subtopics.title: Compressions, Rarefactions and the Longitudinal Wave

questions.question: In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium vibrate:
options: Parallel to the direction the wave travels
Perpendicular to the direction the wave travels
In circles around the direction of travel
Not at all

questions.question: A compression is a region where:
options: The medium has been removed
Particles are crowded together and pressure and density are higher than normal
Particles are spread apart and pressure is lower than normal
The wave has stopped moving

questions.question: The wavelength of a longitudinal wave is the distance between:
options: A compression and the nearest rarefaction
The two ends of the slinky
Two successive compressions — successive points in phase
The rest position and a compression

questions.question: Which statement about the equations f = 1/T and v = fλ for longitudinal waves is correct?
options: Only f = 1/T still applies
Both need an extra factor for the parallel vibration
Neither applies; longitudinal waves have their own equations
Both apply unchanged — the geometry changes, the mathematics does not

subtopics.title: Sound as a Longitudinal Wave, and the Speed of the Medium

questions.question: A ringing bell sealed in a jar falls silent as the air is pumped out because:
options: The vacuum absorbs the sound
The bell stops vibrating without air
Sound needs particles to form compressions — no medium, no sound
The glass reflects all the sound inward

questions.question: Ranked from fastest to slowest, sound travels through:
options: Solid, liquid, gas — closer, more tightly bound particles pass the disturbance sooner
Gas, liquid, solid
Liquid, solid, gas
All three at the same speed

questions.question: Shouting louder makes the sound leave you:
options: Faster
At the same speed — speed belongs to the medium, not the source
Slower, because the compressions are heavier
Faster only in solids

questions.question: The audible range of a healthy human ear is about:
options: 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
1 Hz to 100 Hz
340 Hz to 1 500 Hz

questions.question: The pitch of a note is determined by the wave's:
options: Amplitude
Speed
Frequency
Waveform

questions.question: Striking the same piano key harder changes:
options: The loudness only — bigger amplitude, identical pitch
The pitch only
Both pitch and loudness
The speed of the sound in the room

questions.question: You recognise a saxophone and a flute playing the same note by their:
options: Frequency
Amplitude
Speed
Quality — the waveform shaped by the mix of fainter higher frequencies

questions.question: A siren sounds 680 Hz in air where sound travels at 340 m·s⁻¹. The wavelength is:
options: 2 m

subtopics.title: Echoes, Ultrasound, and the Factor of Two

questions.question: In every echo calculation, the measured time covers:
options: The distance to the reflector only
Half the distance to the reflector
Twice the distance to the reflector — the sound goes there and back
The wavelength of the sound

questions.question: A clap echoes off a quarry wall after 0,9 s, with sound at 340 m·s⁻¹. The wall is:
options: 306 m away
378 m away
170 m away

questions.question: A sonar echo returns to a boat after 0,6 s through seawater at 1 500 m·s⁻¹. The depth is:
options: 450 m — halve the 900 m round trip

questions.question: Ultrasound is preferred over X-rays for scanning an unborn baby because ultrasound:
options: Is not ionising radiation, so it does not damage cells
Travels faster than X-rays
Produces sharper images in every case
Is cheaper to switch on

subtopics.title: The Slinky and the Taxi Queue

questions.question: When the squash travels up the taxi queue, each person:
options: Walks to the front of the queue
Rocks forward and settles back into their own spot
Steps sideways out of the line
Stays perfectly still

questions.question: The queue wave is longitudinal because the people move:
options: Up and down while the squash moves forward
In circles as the squash passes
Along the same line the squash travels
Faster than the squash

questions.question: In the queue picture, one wavelength is the distance from:
options: One squash to the next squash
A squash to the nearest gap
The back of the queue to the front
One person to their neighbour

subtopics.title: Why Sound Is a Queue of Air

questions.question: What arrives at your eardrum when you hear a sound?
options: A stream of air blown from the source
A travelling squash of air — a compression — that presses the drum inward
Individual molecules from the source itself
An electric signal through the air

questions.question: Movies with roaring explosions in space are wrong because:
options: Explosions cannot happen in space
Sound in space is too high to hear
Space is too cold for sound
Space has no particles to squash, so no sound can travel

questions.question: Sound travels fastest through steel because its particles are:
options: Packed shoulder to shoulder and tightly bound, passing the squash on almost instantly
Free to fly across large gaps
Heavier than air molecules
Electrically charged

questions.question: You see lightning well before you hear the thunder because:
options: Thunder happens after the lightning
Light arrives almost instantly while sound plods along at about 340 m·s⁻¹
Thunder must echo off clouds first
The eye reacts faster than the ear

subtopics.title: High, Loud, and the Round Trip

questions.question: Pitch is how OFTEN the squashes arrive; loudness is how HARD they arrive. These match:
options: Frequency and amplitude
Amplitude and frequency
Speed and wavelength
Wavelength and period

questions.question: A clap returns from the quarry wall after 0,9 s. Writing 306 m as the final answer is wrong because:
options: The speed of sound was rounded
306 m is the round trip — the wall is at 153 m
The clap was too soft to measure
Echo times cannot be trusted

questions.question: What makes a bat's hunting squeak ultrasound?
options: It is louder than human speech
It travels faster than normal sound
Its frequency lies above about 20 000 Hz, beyond human hearing
It only works in the dark

questions.question: You recognise a familiar voice at the same pitch and volume as another because of its:
options: Amplitude
Speed
Frequency
Quality — the particular mixture of tones shaping the wave
